name: gason
workload: Parses three real-world JSON files (big.json with heavy escape sequences, monster.json 3D model with many numbers, data.json with many objects) and sums all numeric values, timed in microseconds on desktop and mobile CPUs
claimed_speedup: gason 924us vs RapidJSON 2210us on monster.json (~2.4x, derived from page data); gason 75us vs RapidJSON 91us on data.json (~1.2x, derived from page data); RapidJSON is actually faster than gason on big.json (18093us vs 20092us)
compiler_and_flags: clang-500.2.79 for the OSX/i7 run, gcc 4.8.2 for the Android run; built via 'cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DSHOOTOUT=ON' (exact optimization flags beyond the Release preset are not stated)
hardware: Intel Core i7 2.3GHz, OSX 10.9 (desktop); Samsung Galaxy Note II (GT-N7100), Android 4.3 (mobile)
tradeoffs: Destructive/in-situ parser that mutates the source buffer; objects/arrays are singly-linked lists (no random access); uses NaN-boxing for values; not a strict parser (accepts trailing commas)
caveats: Benchmark numbers are from a 2013-2014 era shootout and unchanged since; results are mixed rather than a clean win (RapidJSON wins on the escape-heavy big.json file); no explicit compiler optimization flags beyond the CMake Release preset
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "json" "SIMD" --sort updated, then opened repos/vivkin/gason/readme via gh api

name: jsmn
workload: General claim of being the fastest JSON tokenizer for embedded/resource-limited use; no specific benchmark dataset or numbers are given in the README
claimed_speedup: "jsmn ... is a world fastest JSON parser/tokenizer" (verbatim project description); no numeric figures provided
tradeoffs: Tokenizer only (no value conversion), zero dynamic allocation, tokens are boundary pointers into the source buffer rather than a DOM; C89, no libc dependency, designed for embedded/AVR/ARM targets
caveats: The project does not name a specific competitor it benchmarked against; 'fastest' is an unsubstantiated first-party claim with zero numbers, included only because the project is highly notable (4k+ stars) per the tier-D notability rule
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "fastest json" --sort stars

name: qajson4c
workload: miloyip/nativejson-benchmark shootout: parses/generates the suite's standard JSON test files across many C/C++ JSON libraries (including RapidJSON and nlohmann/json), measuring parse time, memory footprint, peak memory, and allocation count
claimed_speedup: "Top scores at the nativejson-benchmark on category Parsing Memory, Parsing Memory Peak and AllocCount while scoring quite well at Parsing Time" (verbatim from README); no specific ratio given
stars_or_usage: 10 stars; included as a submodule/test target in the well-known miloyip/nativejson-benchmark shootout
tradeoffs: No dynamic memory allocation required (buffer-based, caller-managed memory), aimed at embedded/memory-constrained targets; lower-level API than DOM-style libraries
caveats: qajson4c's own README admits its nativejson-benchmark result images are outdated ('the pictures are not yet updated'); this session confirmed qajson4c is indeed wired into the nativejson-benchmark suite (src/cjsonlibs/qajson4c_all.c, src/tests/qajson4ctest.cpp) but did not extract fresh numeric results, so the claim is qualitative only
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "json library" language:C --sort stars; cross-checked via gh api search/code?q=qajson4c+repo:miloyip/nativejson-benchmark

name: JSONSki
workload: JSONPath query evaluation over ~1GB single-record and small-record JSON datasets (Twitter, BestBuy, Google Maps Directions, UK NSPL, Walmart, Wikipedia) across 12 distinct JSONPath queries, measuring end-to-end execution time including any preprocessing/parsing
claimed_speedup: "JSONSki runs over 12x faster over ... JPStream ... JSONSki is about 3x faster than Pison, and more than 4x faster than simdjson" for a single large record (verbatim from README); RapidJSON is also included in the comparison chart
compiler_and_flags: g++ 7.4.0 or higher (minimum version stated; exact optimization flags used for the benchmark run are not given)
hardware: Two Intel Xeon E5-2620 v4 @2.1GHz, 128GB RAM, Linux (requires 64-bit ALU, 256-bit SIMD, and pclmulqdq)
stars_or_usage: 33 stars; ASPLOS 2022 Best Paper Award winner
tradeoffs: Supports only a subset of JSONPath (no filter expressions, recursive descent '..', or multi-index arrays); requires Linux plus specific SIMD/pclmulqdq CPU support; streaming API is lower-level than a DOM library
caveats: Numbers are the project's own summary of its peer-reviewed ASPLOS'22 paper; exact compiler optimization flags are not stated; comparison datasets/results predate 2022 and were not re-run against current simdjson/RapidJSON releases in this session
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "JSONPath" language:C++ --sort stars

name: Pison
workload: Parallel structural-index construction plus JSONPath query evaluation over ~1GB single JSON records (Twitter, BestBuy, Google Maps Directions, UK NSPL, Walmart, Wikipedia datasets) on 16-core and 4-core Xeon servers
claimed_speedup: "Parallel Pison achieves 5.4X and 3.1X speedups (on average) over simdjson on Server 1 (with 8 threads) and Server 2 (with 4 threads), respectively"; "both Pison and simdjson outperform RapidJSON" (verbatim from README)
compiler_and_flags: g++ 7.4.0 or higher (minimum version stated; exact optimization flags used for the benchmark run are not given)
hardware: Server 1: 16-core, two Intel Xeon E5-2620 v4 @2.1GHz, 64GB RAM; Server 2: 4-core Intel Xeon E3-1240 v5 @3.5GHz, 16GB RAM
tradeoffs: Requires Linux plus a CPU with pclmulqdq/256-bit SIMD; builds a leveled bitmap structural index rather than a full DOM, so the downstream query API differs from RapidJSON/simdjson; parallel speedup depends on having large single records and enough cores
caveats: Benchmark hardware and datasets are from the original 2021 paper (Xeon E5-2620v4/E3-1240v5) and were not re-verified against current simdjson versions in this session; exact compiler flags unstated
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "JSONPath" language:C++ --sort stars (cross-referenced from the JSONSki README's related-work links)

name: sajson
workload: In-place, single-allocation DOM-style JSON parsing, benchmarked by the author across several platforms (a high-clocked Haswell desktop with MSVC/MinGW, a low-clocked Broadwell Dell XPS 13 on Linux/GCC, an iPhone SE, and an Atom D2700); exact test files/sizes are not itemized in the README
claimed_speedup: "sajson's performance is excellent - it frequently benchmarks faster than RapidJSON, for example" (verbatim from README); the linked blog post shows charts but the numeric MB/s figures are embedded in images and could not be extracted as text
hardware: Per the author's blog: high-clocked Haswell desktop (MSVC and MinGW), Dell XPS 13 low-clocked Broadwell (Linux/GCC), iPhone SE, Atom D2700 (not itemized in the GitHub README itself)
tradeoffs: In-situ parser that mutates the input buffer; no UTF-16/UTF-32 support; no 64-bit integer type; single-allocation mode requires sizing the worst-case output buffer up front
caveats: No numeric speedup figures appear as text on the README; the author's referenced blog post ('Writing a Fast JSON Parser') contains benchmark charts but the values are rendered as images, so no specific ratio is reported here to avoid inventing a number
found_via: WebSearch: "faster than nlohmann OR faster than RapidJSON github JSON parser C++ 2025 2026"
